3 Diffusion-State Policy Optimization
[id=S3.p1.1] In this section,
we propose Diffusion-State Policy Optimization (DiSPO), which performs policy optimization at intermediate diffusion states of MDLMs.
At selected partially-masked states, DiSPO resamples mask fillings from rollout-cached logits to form same-state counterfactual completions, scores them with the same terminal reward, and backpropagates gradients only through the newly filled tokens—without additional rollout forward passes.
DiSPO is a plug-in credit-assignment layer composable with any terminal-feedback objective; in this paper we instantiate the terminal term with diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b).
Algo. 1 summarizes the training procedure.
[id=S3.SS1]
3.1 RL Formulation
[id=S3.SS1.p1.1] States.
For a prompt q∼𝒟q\!\sim\!\mathcal{D} and behavior parameters θold\theta_{\text{old}}, a multi-step MDLM sampler produces a trajectory of partially-masked sequences
xk,1,xk,2,…,xk,Tx_{k,1},x_{k,2},\dots,x_{k,T}, where TT is the number of denoising steps and kk indexes trajectories.
Each xk,t∈(𝒱∪{[MASK]})Lx_{k,t}\!\in\!(\mathcal{V}\!\cup\!\{\texttt{[MASK]}\})^{L} is a length-LL sequence with a subset of positions masked.
Let
[id=S3.Ex3]
Mk,t={i:xk,t,i=[MASK]},Uk,t=[L]∖Mk,t,M_{k,t}=\{i:\,x_{k,t,i}=\texttt{[MASK]}\},\quad U_{k,t}=[L]\setminus M_{k,t},
[id=S3.SS1.p1.2] and define the diffusion state at step tt as sk,t=(q,xk,t)s_{k,t}=(q,x_{k,t}).
[id=S3.SS1.p2.1] Actions and policy factorization.
At state sk,ts_{k,t}, the MDLM outputs logits for all i∈Mk,ti\in M_{k,t}, inducing per-position token distributions πθ(⋅∣sk,t,i)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!s_{k,t},i).
We define the action as the joint filling of the currently masked positions,
ak,t={ak,t,i}i∈Mk,ta_{k,t}=\{a_{k,t,i}\}_{i\in M_{k,t}}, with the factorized policy
[id=S3.E2]
πθ​(ak,t∣sk,t)=∏i∈Mk,tπθ​(ak,t,i∣sk,t,i).\pi_{\theta}(a_{k,t}\mid s_{k,t})\;=\;\prod_{i\in M_{k,t}}\pi_{\theta}\bigl(a_{k,t,i}\mid s_{k,t},i\bigr).
(2)
[id=S3.SS1.p2.2] Applying an action yields a completion deterministically:
o=Fill​(xk,t,ak,t)o=\textsc{Fill}(x_{k,t},a_{k,t}), which replaces xk,t,ix_{k,t,i} by ak,t,ia_{k,t,i} for i∈Mk,ti\in M_{k,t} and keeps Uk,tU_{k,t} fixed.
This state–action view makes it natural to evaluate intermediate decisions using the same terminal reward R⁡(q,o)R(q,o).
Moreover, DiSPO attributes gradients only to the action distribution πθ​(ak,t∣sk,t)\pi_{\theta}(a_{k,t}\mid s_{k,t}), i.e., the newly filled tokens on Mk,tM_{k,t}, treating previously filled tokens as part of the state.
In practice, likelihood ratios and KL terms are computed with a tractable masked-token surrogate introduced in § 3.3.
[id=S3.SS2]
3.2 Per-state Branching and Rewards
[id=S3.SS2.p1.1] For each prompt q∼𝒟q\!\sim\!\mathcal{D}, we first sample KK behavior trajectories by running the multi-step MDLM sampler with frozen parameters θold\theta_{\text{old}},
obtaining {xk,1:T}k=1K\{x_{k,1:T}\}_{k=1}^{K} and terminal completions ok=xk,To_{k}\!=\!x_{k,T}.
During rollout, we cache the logits for each masked position i∈Mk,ti\!\in\!M_{k,t} at every visited state sk,ts_{k,t}.
[id=S3.SS2.p2.1] We then select a set of state indices 𝒮⊆{(k,t)}\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{(k,t)\} to update.
For each selected (k,t)∈𝒮(k,t)\in\mathcal{S}, we form a state-conditioned group by branching from the state:
using cached logits at sk,ts_{k,t}, we resample ZZ actions
[id=S3.Ex4]
ak,t,1,…,ak,t,Z∼πθold(⋅∣sk,t)=∏i∈Mk,tπθold(⋅∣sk,t,i),a_{k,t,1},\dots,a_{k,t,Z}\!\sim\!\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\!\mid\!s_{k,t})\!=\!\prod_{i\in M_{k,t}}\!\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\!\mid\!s_{k,t},i),
[id=S3.SS2.p2.2] and obtain completions ok,t,z=Fill​(xk,t,ak,t,z)o_{k,t,z}\!=\!\textsc{Fill}(x_{k,t},a_{k,t,z}).
Since branching reuses rollout-cached logits, generating these ZZ completions incurs no additional rollout forward passes.
[id=S3.SS2.p3.1] Each completion is scored by the same terminal reward function,
[id=S3.Ex5]
Rk,t,z=R⁡(q,ok,t,z),R_{k,t,z}=R(q,o_{k,t,z}),
[id=S3.SS2.p3.2] and we compute a per-state baseline and group-relative advantages:
[id=S3.E3]
R¯k,t=1Z​∑z=1ZRk,t,z,Ak,t,z=Rk,t,z−R¯k,t.\bar{R}_{k,t}=\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}R_{k,t,z},\quad A_{k,t,z}=R_{k,t,z}-\bar{R}_{k,t}.
(3)
[id=S3.SS2.p3.3] These advantages capture state-conditioned preferences over alternative fillings under a fixed intermediate state.
[id=S3.SS3]
3.3 Step-level Surrogate Log-probabilities
[id=S3.SS3.p1.1] To optimize masked-token actions at intermediate states, we need tractable log-probabilities to form likelihood ratios for the diffusion-state policy.
Following Zhao et al. (2025b), we use a one-step masked-token surrogate π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} (Eq. 1), and adapt it to a state-wise definition that accounts only for the currently masked positions.
[id=S3.SS3.p2.1] State-wise masked-token surrogate.
For each state sk,t=(q,xk,t)s_{k,t}=(q,x_{k,t}), sample a random prompt-masking pattern mm to obtain a corrupted prompt q(m)q^{(m)} and define
sk,t(m)=(q(m),xk,t)s_{k,t}^{(m)}\!=\!(q^{(m)},x_{k,t}).
Running a single denoising step on sk,t(m)s_{k,t}^{(m)} yields per-position distributions π~θ(⋅∣sk,t(m),i)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\!\mid\!s_{k,t}^{(m)},i) for all i∈Mk,ti\in M_{k,t}.
For an action sample ak,t,za_{k,t,z}, define the state-wise surrogate log-probability by summing over actionable positions:
[id=S3.E4]
log⁡π~θ​(ak,t,z∣sk,t):=𝔼m​[∑i∈Mk,tlog⁡π~θ​(ak,t,z,i∣sk,t(m),i)].\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{k,t,z}\!\mid\!s_{k,t})\!:=\!\mathbb{E}_{m}\!\!\left[\sum_{i\in M_{k,t}}\!\!\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}\bigl(a_{k,t,z,i}\!\mid\!s_{k,t}^{(m)}\!,\!i\bigr)\right].
(4)
[id=S3.SS3.p2.2] This restriction makes the update token-local: rewards computed from completions affect only the newly filled tokens at the current state.
[id=S3.SS3.p3.1] Implementation note.
We estimate the expectation over mm with the same Monte Carlo scheme as Zhao et al. (2025b).
All log-probabilities, likelihood ratios, and KL terms in our objectives are computed using π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}.
[id=S3.SS4]
3.4 Training Objective
[id=S3.SS4.p1.1] For clarity, we present the unclipped likelihood-ratio objectives; our implementation uses standard clipping and a KL penalty to a reference surrogate policy π~ref\tilde{\pi}_{\text{ref}}.
[id=S3.SS4.p2.1] State-wise objective.
For each selected state (k,t)∈𝒮(k,t)\in\mathcal{S}, we have ZZ action samples with rewards {(ak,t,z,Rk,t,z)}z=1Z\{(a_{k,t,z},R_{k,t,z})\}_{z=1}^{Z} and advantages from Eq. 3.
Using the state-wise surrogate (Eq. 4), define the likelihood ratio
[id=S3.Ex6]
ρk,t,z​(θ)=exp⁡(log⁡π~θ​(ak,t,z∣sk,t)−log⁡π~θold​(ak,t,z∣sk,t)).\rho_{k,t,z}(\theta)\!=\!\exp\!\Bigl(\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{k,t,z}\!\mid\!s_{k,t})-\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{k,t,z}\!\mid\!s_{k,t})\Bigr).
[id=S3.SS4.p2.2] The step-level loss at (k,t)(k,t) is
[id=S3.E5]
ℒstep(k,t)(θ)=−1Z∑z=1Zρk,t,z(θ)Ak,t,z,\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(k,t)}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{Z}\sum\nolimits_{z=1}^{Z}\rho_{k,t,z}(\theta)\,A_{k,t,z},
(5)
[id=S3.SS4.p2.3] and the aggregated step-level loss is
[id=S3.E6]
ℒstep​(θ)=∑(k,t)∈𝒮ℒstep(k,t)​(θ).{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)}=\sum\nolimits_{(k,t)\in\mathcal{S}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(k,t)}(\theta).
(6)
[id=S3.SS4.p3.1] Terminal objective.
The step-wise objective can be combined with any terminal-feedback policy-optimization objective on final completions.
In this paper, for controlled comparison, we instantiate it with diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b).
For each prompt qq, rollout completions {ok}k=1K\{o_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} are scored by rk=R⁡(q,ok)r_{k}=R(q,o_{k}) and converted to group-relative advantages using r¯q=1K​∑k=1Krk\bar{r}_{q}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_{k}.
Using the sequence-level surrogate log-probabilities log⁡π~θ​(q,ok)\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(q,o_{k}) (Eq. 1), define
[id=S3.Ex7]
ρk​(θ)=exp⁡(log⁡π~θ​(q,ok)−log⁡π~θold​(q,ok)),\rho_{k}(\theta)=\exp\!\Bigl(\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(q,o_{k})-\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(q,o_{k})\Bigr),
[id=S3.SS4.p3.2] The terminal loss is
[id=S3.E7]
ℒterm(θ)=−1K∑k=1Kρk(θ)Ak.{\color[rgb]{0.21,0.12,1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta)}=-\frac{1}{K}\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{k}(\theta)\,A_{k}.
(7)
[id=S3.SS4.p4.1] Combined objective.
We optimize a weighted combination of step-wise and terminal objectives:
[id=S3.E8]
ℒ⁡(θ)=αterm​ℒterm​(θ)+αstep​ℒstep​(θ),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\alpha_{\text{term}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.21,0.12,1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta)}+\alpha_{\text{step}}\,{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)},
(8)
[id=S3.SS4.p4.2] where αstep,αterm∈ℝ≥0\alpha_{\text{step}},\alpha_{\text{term}}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}.
We set αterm=1\alpha_{\text{term}}\!=\!1 in experiments.

4 Theoretical Analysis
[id=S4.p1.1] DiSPO treats intermediate diffusion states as decision points and directly optimizes their mask fillings via policy gradients.
Under the masked-token surrogate policy π~θ\tilde{\pi}_{\theta} (Eq. 4),
we show that the step-wise loss provides a principled policy-gradient estimator for a fixed-state objective (Theorem 4.1).
We further show that combining step-wise and terminal losses corresponds in expectation to optimizing a single objective (Theorem 4.2).
We also provide simple variance-reduction mechanisms that justify token-local updates and same-state averaging (§4.3).
For clarity, we analyze the unclipped likelihood-ratio objective without KL.
[id=S4.SS1]
4.1 Step-wise Objective and Step-level Policy Gradient
[id=S4.SS1.p1.1] Fix a denoising step index tt.
Let dt​(q)d_{t}(q) denote the distribution over intermediate states at step tt induced by rolling out the frozen behavior model θold\theta_{\text{old}} on prompts q∼𝒟q\sim\mathcal{D}.
Using the state–action view in §3.1, define
[id=S4.E9]
Jt(θ):=𝔼q∼𝒟𝔼st∼dt​(q)𝔼a∼π~θ(⋅∣st)[R(q,Fill(xt,a))],J_{t}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{s_{t}\sim d_{t}(q)}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})}\bigl[R\bigl(q,\textsc{Fill}(x_{t},a)\bigr)\bigr],
(9)
[id=S4.SS1.p1.2] where st=(q,xt)s_{t}=(q,x_{t}) and Fill​(xt,a)\textsc{Fill}(x_{t},a) deterministically completes xtx_{t} by filling its masked positions with aa.
Theorem 4.1 (Principled step-level policy gradient).
[id=S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.1] Assume (i) dt​(q)d_{t}(q) is independent of θ\theta, and (ii) π~θ(⋅∣s)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s) is differentiable and normalized for each ss.
Using the within-group mean baseline in Eq. 3, in the unclipped likelihood-ratio setting the expected gradient of the step-wise loss is aligned with the policy gradient of Jt​(θ)J_{t}(\theta):
[id=S4.E10]
𝔼⁡[−∇θℒstep(t)​(θ)]=Z−1Z​∇θJt​(θ).\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}^{(t)}(\theta)\bigr]=\frac{Z-1}{Z}\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta).
(10)
[id=S4.SS1.p2.1] Proof idea.
Write the step-wise loss (Eq. 5) as a score-function estimator for π~θ​(a∣st)\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t}) using action-only log-probabilities on the current mask.
The likelihood-ratio form gives the standard importance-weighted policy gradient; the within-group mean baseline induces only the constant factor (Z−1)/Z(Z-1)/Z in expectation and reduces variance.
Full details are in Appendix A.1.
[id=S4.SS2]
4.2 Mixed Objective and Overall Policy Gradient
[id=S4.SS2.p1.1] A key property of DiSPO is that adding step-wise updates does not introduce an ad-hoc signal: in the unclipped, exact likelihood-ratio setting, the expected gradient of the combined loss (Eq. 8) equals the gradient of a single well-defined objective.
[id=S4.SS2.p2.1] Terminal surrogate objective.
Define the terminal (sequence-level) surrogate objective
[id=S4.E11]
Jseq(θ):=𝔼q∼𝒟,o∼π~θ(⋅∣q)[R(q,o)].J_{\text{seq}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D},\,o\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)}\bigl[R(q,o)\bigr].
(11)
[id=S4.SS2.p2.2] A standard likelihood-ratio argument implies that the unclipped terminal loss ℒterm​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta) is an unbiased policy-gradient estimator for Jseq​(θ)J_{\text{seq}}(\theta) (Shao et al., 2024).
[id=S4.SS2.p3.1] Mixed objective.
Let cZ:=(Z−1)/Zc_{Z}:=(Z-1)/Z denote the constant scaling induced by the within-group mean baseline in Eq. 3.
With timestep sampling ω⁡(t)\omega(t) and the step-wise objectives {Jt​(θ)}\{J_{t}(\theta)\} (Eq. 9), define
[id=S4.E12]
Jmix​(θ):=αstep​cZ​∑tω⁡(t)​Jt​(θ)+αterm​Jseq​(θ).J_{\text{mix}}(\theta):=\alpha_{\text{step}}\,c_{Z}\sum_{t}\omega(t)\,J_{t}(\theta)+\alpha_{\text{term}}\,J_{\text{seq}}(\theta).
(12)
Theorem 4.2 (Overall policy gradient).
[id=S4.Thmtheorem2.p1.1] Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.1 (with the within-group mean baseline) and the standard likelihood-ratio assumptions for Jseq​(θ)J_{\text{seq}}(\theta),
[id=S4.E13]
𝔼⁡[−∇θℒ​(θ)]=∇θJmix​(θ),\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\bigr]=\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{mix}}(\theta),
(13)
[id=S4.Thmtheorem2.p1.2] where ℒ⁡(θ)=αstep​ℒstep​(θ)+αterm​ℒterm​(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\alpha_{\text{step}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)+\alpha_{\text{term}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta).
[id=S4.SS2.p4.1] Proof idea.
Condition on a timestep tt: Theorem 4.1 gives 𝔼⁡[−∇θℒstep​(θ)∣t]=cZ​∇θJt​(θ)\mathbb{E}[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}}(\theta)\mid t]=c_{Z}\,\nabla_{\theta}J_{t}(\theta).

Then add 𝔼⁡[−∇θℒterm​(θ)]=∇θJseq​(θ)\mathbb{E}[-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}}(\theta)]=\nabla_{\theta}J_{\text{seq}}(\theta) and use linearity of expectation.
See Appendix A.2 for details.
[id=S4.SS3]
4.3 Variance Reduction for the State-wise Estimator
[id=S4.SS3.p1.1] DiSPO uses two simple mechanisms that reduce the variance of DiSPOś state-wise gradient estimates: (i) restricting gradients to actionable (masked) tokens, and (ii) averaging over ZZ candidates per state via cached-logit resampling.
[id=S4.SS3.p2.1] Token-local updates.
Fix a state s=(q,x)s=(q,x) of length LL with masked set MM of size m=|M|m=|M|, and let RR be the terminal reward of the resulting completion.
Let gi:=∇θ​log​π~θ​(ai∣s,i)g_{i}:=\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{i}\mid s,i) denote a per-position score term.
Compare an estimator that propagates through all positions,
g^full:=∑i=1Lgi​R\hat{g}_{\text{full}}:=\sum_{i=1}^{L}g_{i}\,R,
to the action-only estimator,
g^sub:=∑i∈Mgi​R\hat{g}_{\text{sub}}:=\sum_{i\in M}g_{i}\,R.
Proposition 4.3 (Variance reduction by partial updates).
[id=S4.Thmtheorem3.p1.1] Assume {gi}\{g_{i}\} are independent, zero-mean with Var⁡[gi]=σ2\mathrm{Var}[g_{i}]=\sigma^{2}, and RR is independent of {gi}\{g_{i}\} with 𝔼⁡[R2]<∞\mathbb{E}[R^{2}]<\infty.
Then
[id=S4.Ex8]
Var⁡[g^sub]≤mL​Var​[g^full].\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{\text{sub}}]\leq\frac{m}{L}\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}_{\text{full}}].
[id=S4.SS3.p3.1] Proof idea.
Under the assumptions, the variance of the sum scales linearly with the number of included positions, giving the factor m/Lm/L.
See Appendix A.3.
[id=S4.SS3.p4.1] Same-state averaging via cached-logit branching.
At a fixed state ss, DiSPO can resample ZZ independent branches and average their gradient contributions.
With any baseline b⁡(s)b(s) that is independent of each sampled action, the variance of the averaged estimator decreases at the standard O⁡(1/Z)O(1/Z) rate.
Cached-logit branching avoids additional rollout forward passes to obtain these ZZ samples.
Proposition 4.4 (Variance vs. number of drafts).
[id=S4.Thmtheorem4.p1.1] Fix a state ss and draw i.i.d. actions a1,…,aZ∼π~θ(⋅∣s)a_{1},\dots,a_{Z}\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s) with rewards RzR_{z}.
Let b⁡(s)b(s) be any baseline independent of each aza_{z}, and define the per-branch contribution
g^z:=(Rz−b⁡(s))​∇θ​log⁡π~θ​(az∣s)\hat{g}_{z}:=(R_{z}-b(s))\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\tilde{\pi}_{\theta}(a_{z}\mid s) with finite variance.
Then the averaged estimator Var⁡[g^]=O⁡(1/Z)\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}]=O(1/Z).
[id=S4.SS3.p5.1] Proof idea.
The estimator is the average of ZZ i.i.d. per-branch terms under an action-independent baseline, so its variance shrinks by 1/Z1/Z.
See Appendix A.4.
[id=S4.SS3.p6.1] Remark (group-relative baseline used in practice).
Our implementation uses the within-group mean baseline (Eq. 3), which introduces dependence across branches but typically further reduces variance in practice; we empirically verify variance reduction from increasing ZZ (§ 5).

5 Experiments
[id=S5.p1.1] This section evaluates whether incorporating intermediate-state updates improves policy optimization for MDLMs.
Since DiSPO naturally augments terminal-feedback optimization with a state-wise objective (Algo. 1; Eq. 18),
we use the most direct baseline: diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b).
To isolate the effect of state-conditioned credit assignment,
we match training budgets by fixing
i) the number of full diffusion rollouts,
ii) the sequence-level group size,
and iii) the number of RL update steps;
DiSPO resamples by reusing cached-logit within each rollout.
[id=S5.SS1]
5.1 Setup
[id=S5.SS1.p1.1] Models.
We evaluate LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Nie et al., 2025) and a variant further fine-tuned on s1k (Muennighoff et al., 2025).
Across methods, we follow the identical fine-tuning and RL recipe of Zhao et al. (2025b) and keep the denoising schedule fixed. See Appendix B.3 for more details.
[id=S5.SS1.p2.1] Benchmarks and metrics.
Following Zhao et al. (2025b), we report exact-match accuracy on benchmarks for math reasoning (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021); MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2023)) and symbolic planning (Sudoku; Countdown (Zhao et al., 2025b)).
See Appendix B.1 for details.
[id=S5.SS1.p3.1] Optimization.
For fair comparison, we match the baseline training setup across methods (including Ngen=256N_{\text{gen}}{=}256, denoising schedule, rollout budget, and the number of RL updates) and reuse the same terminal reward evaluator for both terminal and state-wise terms.
Unless stated otherwise, DiSPO uses Z=2Z{=}2, samples one timestep per rollout from a late-biased polynomial distribution (degree k=4k{=}4), and sets αstep=0.1\alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0.1; remaining hyperparameters are in Appendix B.3.
[id=S5.SS1.p4.1] Evaluation.
We follow the protocol of diffu-GRPO (Zhao et al., 2025b).
We evaluate at Ngen∈{128,256,512}N_{\text{gen}}\in\{128,256,512\} using zero-shot greedy decoding.
For diffusion decoding, we use Ngen/2N_{\text{gen}}/2 denoising steps with a block size of 32 tokens.
We provide more details in Appendix B.2.

[id=S5.SS2.p1.1] Table 1 reports exact-match accuracy on four benchmarks for Ngen∈{128,256,512}N_{\text{gen}}\!\in\!\{128,256,512\}.
At the default generation length (Ngen=256N_{\text{gen}}{=}256), DiSPO outperforms terminal-feedback diffu-GRPO across all model–benchmark pairs, with gains largely persisting at other generation lengths, including Avg.
[id=S5.SS2.p2.1] Importantly, these gains are obtained under matched rollout forward passes and parameter-update steps, using the same terminal reward evaluator for both terminal and state-wise updates.
This suggests the improvements come from finer-grained, state-wise credit assignment rather than extra rollouts or additional reward shaping.
[id=S5.SS2.p3.1] To probe the underlying training dynamics, Fig. 2 plots both terminal rewards (top) and step rewards (bottom) on LLaDA-8B-Instruct.
DiSPO reaches higher terminal rewards earlier and sustains them throughout training; while step rewards vary over a smaller range, they track the up and downs of terminal reward, consistent with a state-wise signal that aligns with terminal feedback along the trajectory.

5.3 Analysis: State-wise Estimator Design
[id=S5.SS3.p1.1] Propositions 4.3 and 4.4 motivate two variance-reduction choices for intermediate-state policy optimization: (A) updating only actionable (newly filled) tokens and (B) averaging over ZZ same-state drafts.
We evaluate both on 4×\times4 Sudoku via lightweight, controlled comparisons of step-wise gradient variance and task performance.
[id=S5.SS3.p2.1] Empirical verification of gradient variance.
To test the variance predictions, we measure the variance of the state-wise gradient estimator.
At the last checkpoint for LLaDA-8B-Instruct in Sudoku, we repeatedly resample rollouts from the same set of states and estimate the trace covariance of the resulting state-wise gradient estimates, trCov⁡(g^)\mathrm{trCov}(\hat{g}).
Figure 3 shows that (left) switching from all-token to actionable-token updates at Z=2Z{=}2 reduces trCov⁡(g^)\mathrm{trCov}(\hat{g}), and (right) increasing ZZ under actionable-only updates reduces it, consistent with Propositions 4.3 and 4.4 (Appendix C).
[id=S5.SS3.p3.1] Impact on task performance.
We then assess how these choices affect accuracy under the same training budget.
Table 2 (top) shows that updating all tokens underperforms the actionable-only, supporting alignment with the state–action decomposition.
Sweeping Z∈{2,3,4}Z\in\{2,3,4\} (bottom), we observe occasional gains at specific NgenN_{\text{gen}} but no monotonic improvement in average; we therefore use Z=2Z{=}2 by default.

5.4 Ablations: Optimization Recipe
[id=S5.SS4.p1.1] We ablate three design choices for optimization:
(i) which intermediate states to train on,
(ii) the optimization objective,
and (iii) weight for the step-wise objective (αstep\alpha_{\text{step}}).
[id=S5.SS4.p2.1] Timestep sampling.
We compare uniform sampling to polynomial samplers (k=4k{=}4) that bias draws toward late timesteps (near terminal states) or early timesteps (its mirrored variant).
Table 3 (top) shows that late-biased sampling performs best, suggesting that very early masked states are too noisy for reliable credit assignment.
[id=S5.SS4.p3.1] Objectives.
Table 3 (middle) shows that ℒstep\mathcal{L}_{\text{step}} alone outperforms ℒterm\mathcal{L}_{\text{term}} alone, and combining them performs best, indicating complementary learning signals.
[id=S5.SS4.p4.1] Intermediate-state weight.
Table 3 (bottom) shows that,
sweeping αstep∈{0.1,0.5,0.9}\alpha_{\text{step}}\!\in\!\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}, performance consistently stays above αstep=0\alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0.
However, gains are non-monotonic (best at αstep=0.5\alpha_{\text{step}}{=}0.5), indicating its optimisation potential.
[id=S5.SS5]
5.5 Error Analysis: Early Commitments
[id=S5.SS5.p1.1] We analyze early-commitment errors using the final checkpoint of LLaD-8B-Instruct for Sudoku. We use Ngen=128N_{\text{gen}}{=}128; all other settings match the main experiments.
[id=S5.SS5.p2.1] Figure 4 compares the same instance at the same denoising step: diffu-GRPO already violates constraints due to an early incorrect fill, whereas DiSPO maintains a consistent partial assignment.
Figure 5 corroborates this at scale—the first-violation time occurs later with DiSPO.
These indicate that state-wise optimization reduces premature, hard-to-correct commitments during denoising.
[id=S5.SS6]
5.6 Compute Cost Breakdown
[id=S5.SS6.p1.1] Algorithmic overhead.
Table 4 shows per-prompt operation counts.
DiSPO matches the dominant costs—diffusion-rollout forward passes (K​TKT) and optimizer updates (UU)—and adds only lightweight extras: reward evaluations for same-state branches and one-step surrogate calls to compute step-wise log-probs at selected states.
[id=S5.SS6.p2.1] Wall-clock overhead and efficiency.
Our current implementation is slower (∼\sim0.4×\times baseline throughput at Z=2Z{=}2 and |𝒮|=K|\mathcal{S}|{=}K), largely due to non-optimized repeated policy/surrogate calls and kernel/IO overhead; we discuss likely causes and optimizations in Appendix E.
To account for this, Fig. 6 compares wall-clock-matched training curves: although DiSPO starts slower, it catches up and surpasses the terminal-feedback baseline within the same time budget, indicating improved performance per unit time from better credit assignment rather than extra rollout/update compute.

6 Related Work
[id=S6.p1.1] Terminal-feedback policy optimization for MDLMs.
Most RL fine-tuning methods for masked diffusion LMs use a scalar terminal reward on the final completion and perform PPO/GRPO-style updates via surrogate likelihoods (Zhao et al., 2025b; Tang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Rojas et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Zekri and Boullé, 2025; Zhao et al., 2025a).
Our method differs by performing state-conditioned comparisons: at a fixed intermediate state, we contrast alternative mask fillings (actions) rather than only learning from terminal rollouts.
[id=S6.p2.1] State-aware reward shaping.
SAPO scores intermediate denoising states to build step-aware bonuses that shape the terminal signal (Xie et al., 2025), typically requiring additional multi-step rollouts.
In contrast, DiSPO directory optimizes intermediate-state actions without extra rollouts; a reference comparison is provided in Appendix D.
[id=S6.p3.1] Trajectory-level objectives.
MDPO aligns with the denoising trajectory by comparing different rollouts across steps and favoring trajectories whose intermediate predictions improve toward the terminal outcome (He et al., 2025).
In contrast, DiSPO uses a different optimization unit: it fixes an intermediate state and compares alternative mask fillings.
[id=S6.p4.1] Surrogate likelihoods and gradient estimators.
Complementary work improves surrogate likelihoods or policy-gradient estimators for diffusion LMs (Wang et al., 2025a; Zekri and Boullé, 2025; Rojas et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b).
DiSPO can directly incorporate improved surrogates/estimators while keeping the state-wise objective unchanged.
[id=S7]
7 Conclusion
[id=S7.p1.1] We propose DiSPO, a plug-in intermediate-state credit-assignment layer for policy optimization of masked diffusion language models, grounded in a policy-gradient formulation (§ 3).
This formulation induces step-wise and mixed objectives with principled policy-gradient estimators, and we analyze its variance reduction mechanisms (§ 4).
Empirically, instantiating DiSPO on top of terminal-feedback diffu-GRPO, we consistently improve accuracy across math and planning tasks under matched rollout forward passes and update steps using the same terminal reward (§ 5).
[id=S7.p2.1] Limitations and discussion.
DiSPO is a plug-in state-wise credit-assignment layer; future work includes pairing it with other terminal-feedback objectives (e.g., GDPO (Rojas et al., 2025)) and improved surrogate likelihood or gradient estimators (e.g., SPG (Wang et al., 2025a)).
We also use an unshaped terminal reward; studying complementarity with reward shaping (e.g., SAPO (Xie et al., 2025)) would clarify their interaction.
[id=Sx1]
Impact Statement
[id=Sx1.p1.1] This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning by improving policy optimization for masked diffusion language models.
There are many potential societal consequences of improved language-model reasoning capabilities, including both beneficial applications and possible misuse; we do not believe our method introduces unique ethical concerns beyond those common to this line of research.
